# Excerpt library: how the winners say each kind of thing (HVAC)

Short lines from winning HVAC scripts, grouped by the job the line does. Each shows (channel, video ID, [timestamp], views against the channel normal).

**Sources:** real people on camera only. That is 22 of the 36 transcripts in `studies/hvac/data/`, from 12 channels: Atlas AC, Deanin' It Yourself, Everyday Home Repairs (2), Home RenoVision DIY, How To Home (2), HVAC Guide for Homeowners, Silver Cymbal (2), Technology Connections (2), The DIY HVAC Guy (6), The Funny Carpenter, The Provident Prepper and Word of Advice TV (2). By the operator's decision (2026-10-27), no line comes from a faceless, AI-voiced or off-camera video: Ray Dutton's Garage, HVAC Exposed, Vent Exposed, Lost Survival Knowledge, Roger the Pipe Guy and grayfurnaceman are left out, and so is Project Farm's filter test (hands only, no one on camera). WINNI's cold-walls video has no transcript. Views against normal come from `studies/hvac/notes/INDEX.md` (collected 2026-10-27). Normals differ hugely between channels (about 2,000 views on Deanin' It Yourself against about 1.9 million on Technology Connections), so compare a ratio only with others on the same channel.

**How quotes are given:** verbatim auto-captions, checked by script against the transcript. The timestamp is the start of the caption line where the quote begins. "..." marks a cut, and [square brackets] mark an obvious caption fix. Unpunctuated captions read as one long run.

**What to borrow:** real tradesmen and homeowners talking. Borrow the voice and the structure: how plain the line is, how short, and where it sits.

**How to use this file:** to learn the range of shapes each job can take, never to copy wording. Every group holds several shapes. Pick a different one from the last script on the same channel (the rotation log tracks it) and write it fresh from the brief, in the persona's voice. Every fact, price, reading and wait in a script comes from the brief and the price guide, never from a line quoted here. The scanner's copy guard flags any run of 8 or more words shared with this file, so wording is never copied.

**What to leave behind:** these channels have a face, their own hands, a meter and a furnace on camera. Anything that needs the footage ("right here", "like this one", "as you can see", a meter reading), their names, greetings ("Hey guys, Jay here"), sign-offs ("you guys be safe"), stores, sponsors, codes and their own tests stays with them. Roger is faceless and never claims a test or a reading.

**Problem lines:** a few groups end with one or two lines marked **Problem:**. They show what our rules ban (a motive, a tease, pointing at the screen, a test or reading we can't claim, unsafe advice) or what the comments punished. Never use them as a model.

## Contents
1. The point in the first sentence
2. Questions in the opening
3. The villain as a price or a silence
4. Honest scope and reassurance
5. Promise blocks and concrete forward promises
6. Priority flags
7. Item lines by shape (method; rule, reason, verdict; contender verdicts; myth, then truth; the escalation ladder)
8. The mechanism in one plain line
9. Checks the viewer runs at home
10. Money lines
11. Honest limits and candor
12. Safety lines inside the step
13. Call-a-pro lines with a named trigger
14. Forward lines between items
15. Short mid-video CTAs and one-line end reminders
16. Comment questions and endings that ask for a comment
17. Season and the clock
18. Carbon monoxide and gas, in proportion

## 1. The point in the first sentence

The opening's first job: name the title's subject and, wherever the title allows, the part, the setting or the fix itself, by about 15 seconds. Notice that the real channels say the subject plainly, often as the symptom in the viewer's words, that most of them reached their first real value by 45 seconds in the study, and that the fastest reach the first step by 0:11. Borrow the placement and the length; never hold the name back.

1. "Today I want to go over the most common furnace problem. So on average, every for example, every six furnace calls, one of them is guaranteed to be this problem." (Word of Advice TV, 3Jonl_TLkpE, [0:02], 140.71x)
   **Shape:** the subject and how common it is, then "take off the top door" at 0:11. **Watch:** the part (the flame sensor) isn't named until 1:52; name it in the first breath. The greeting before it is banned for us.
2. "I'm going to show you quickly how to troubleshoot and solve a problem where your furnace is turning on and then quickly off and not providing any heat through your vents in your home" (Everyday Home Repairs, sRvH-io-ZtA, [0:01], 9.16x)
   **Shape:** the symptom the viewer is living, said as the subject. 2.78 million views.
3. "the first one is a lot of folks do not consider air flow enough they don't change their air filter enough" (HVAC Guide for Homeowners, Unx9Ze10N98, [0:17], 190.77x)
   **Shape:** item one at 0:17, after a one-line question and the count.
4. "Okay, starting out at number five. Not really a mistake, but it can be really frustrating trying to take out an old filter." (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [0:21], 5.81x)
   **Shape:** the countdown's first item at 0:21, with honest scope ("not really a mistake").
5. "first thing we're gonna start with is a real easy fix so go outside find out where your drain line goes" (Silver Cymbal, qAxJb0J1HH0, [0:27], 46.03x)
   **Shape:** the first step at 0:25, sending the viewer to his own yard.
6. "you've probably heard from all sorts of people that electric space heaters are dangerous things which are likely to cause a fire and it is true they can be dangerous and they can start fires however likely not in the ways you imagine" (Technology Connections, HnMuNCl7tZ8, [0:00], 1.53x)
   **Shape:** the belief, conceded, then turned, all in sentence one.
7. "this is a capacitor and it's like a little battery that gives your AC unit an extra jolt of energy when it first kicks on" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Is0pv2Qnza0, [0:11], 60.42x)
   **Shape:** the part named and its job in one breath. **Watch:** it follows "it involves this right here", a pointer to the screen.

- **Problem:** "in this video I'm going to show you how I go about diagnosing and repairing what is most definitely one of the most common service calls" (How To Home, i8nDBZo6XyE, [0:00], 8.14x)
  A banned opener, the part unnamed until 0:59, and neither of the title's prices ("Was Quoted $400. I Fixed It For $11.72!") said in the spoken hook.

## 2. Questions in the opening

A question the viewer can answer from their own house, their own thermostat or their own choice, answered within about 15 seconds. Notice that the good ones are yes-or-no or a choice, and that the answer follows at once, often in the next sentence. Borrow the placement (first line, or straight after the subject), the length (one sentence) and the quick answer. Never ask something the viewer can't check.

1. "Did you know that you can turn your car into a generator?" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Qx3cC1y23JY, [0:00], 60.44x)
   **Shape:** the question is the point; the price gap answers it in the next sentence (group 10).
2. "hey do you guys have a clogged AC drain and you need to get it flushed you don't want to call a professional this little tool can save you hundreds" (Deanin' It Yourself, dRL13JlclhM, [0:00], 818.48x)
   **Shape:** a yes-or-no about the viewer's own drain, then the pro and the money in words. **Watch:** the tool stays unnamed and a "stay tuned to the end" follows; both are banned for us.
3. "Which ones are better for the air quality in your home? And are the expensive ones actually costing you more electricity than you thought?" (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [0:05], 5.81x)
   **Shape:** two short questions straight after the subject, both answered by the list.
4. "Sounds impossible at first, doesn't it? If it's colder outside than in, what heat is there to take?" (Technology Connections, 7J52mDjZzto, [0:18], 2.51x)
   **Shape:** the disbelief beat, voiced for the viewer, then answered: "But it's very possible".
5. "what is the biggest HVAC mistake we see made in the winter time" (HVAC Guide for Homeowners, Unx9Ze10N98, [0:00], 190.77x)
   **Shape:** the title as a question, answered by the last item, with its stake named at 0:08 (group 5).
6. "do you know how to stay warm during a winter power outage" (The Provident Prepper, erq-QuCN0G0, [0:00], 73.43x)
   **Shape:** the outage question as the whole first line. **Watch:** names, a tease ("stay with us") and the first tip at 1:06 follow; ours answers in 15 seconds.

- **Problem:** "but which on should you go with and which one should you stay away from" (Atlas AC, r_uP9itJ0HQ, [0:12], 88.63x)
  A good choice question, answered at 12:01, behind a like ask, two disclaimers and "you are going to want to watch this to the end".

## 3. The villain as a price or a silence

One line in the opening that aims at the bill, the quote or what nobody mentions, said as a fact the viewer can check against their own invoice. Notice that HVAC viewers name the trade far more than plumbing viewers (about 95 distrust comments against about 34 defences), so the line has to be fair to the honest tech: a tech owning up to what he charges, a quote range, the honest contractor as the way out. Borrow the placement (once, inside the first two minutes, then let the prices carry it) and the length. The store shelf and the sales pitch can stand beside the trade as softer villains. "You need a whole new unit" is the upsell's signature. Never motives.

1. "I've heard of people being charged $2,000 to replace this piece and guess how much it is $10" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Is0pv2Qnza0, [0:21], 60.42x)
   **Shape:** the quote against the part, the second price as a question. Ours gives both as ranges from the price guide, and the comments brought their own ($550 quoted, $18.36 paid, 1K likes).
2. "This thing honestly has made me so much money in my career because I have to go out and charge people to to clean their flame sensor, but I wish more people knew how to do this and it would save them a lot of money." (The DIY HVAC Guy, mP0IjyvQtxw, [10:52], 30.24x)
   **Shape:** the billing fact told by the man who bills it. No motive, only what the call costs.
3. "the profit margins are huge where the supplies cost a little to nothing they're incredibly easy to do and they're also very quick" (How To Home, i8nDBZo6XyE, [11:07], 8.14x)
   **Shape:** the silence explained by the price of the parts and the time, not by anyone's character.
4. "you have all these different contractors telling you which brand is the best and why you should be buying their brand" (Atlas AC, r_uP9itJ0HQ, [0:04], 88.63x)
   **Shape:** the sales pitch as the problem the video solves, from a contractor who then discloses his own brand (group 11).
5. "Don't get hung up on all of these different brands. A lot of these are actually the same equipment. Here is the key. The key is to find a good HVAC contractor that you trust." (The DIY HVAC Guy, x2BK-zr4raE, [6:03], 31.96x)
   **Shape:** the honest tech as the way out, said plainly.
6. "this is one sale that UPC scan symbol probably shouldn't even exist on this box it's very confusing" (Home RenoVision DIY, J95l9Ue4224, [5:00], 24.92x)
   **Shape:** the store as the soft villain, over a practical trap the viewer can avoid.
7. "if you're having a problem with your air conditioning this is a great way to make sure that this is not part of the issue and save yourself a couple hundred dollars in a service call" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [7:09], 52.54x)
   **Shape:** the visit's price as the stake, inside the step, with no one blamed.

- **Problem:** "I don't know how these guys sleep at night" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Is0pv2Qnza0, [0:34], 60.42x)
  A motive. Its video drew the trade's most-liked defence: "We are not all out here to screw you over" (1.6K likes).
- **Problem:** "some of the top things that AC companies do not want you knowing how to do or that you're even allowed to do them" (How To Home, AQQH9QwC46A, [0:01], 11.05x)
  A motive as the frame of the whole video, repeated as its bridge between items. Ours aims at the price and the silence.

## 4. Honest scope and reassurance

One line that keeps the title's strongest word honest: what the fix covers, why the viewer can manage it, or that the problem is smaller than it feels. Notice that the real channels say "you don't need any special tools" and "don't be intimidated" plainly, and that the best reassurance names what the viewer fears (the open cabinet, the rain on the unit). Borrow the placement (inside the opening, straight after the point, or right after an alarming fact) and the length (one sentence, rarely two).

1. "I'm gonna give you three tips that you can do at home yourself you don't need any special tools" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [0:01], 52.54x)
   **Shape:** the count, who does it and the reassurance in sentence one.
2. "with just a little knowledge on common furnace operation you're going to be able to troubleshoot this yourself" (Everyday Home Repairs, sRvH-io-ZtA, [0:11], 9.16x)
   **Shape:** what the viewer needs (knowledge, not tools) and what it lets him do.
3. "but don't be intimidated when you get to your furnace and you see a lot of mechanical things the guts of these furnaces are all pretty much the same" (Everyday Home Repairs, --A2I2s7aNw, [0:43], 7.16x)
   **Shape:** names the fear an older viewer has at the open cabinet, then lowers it.
4. "So, to remedy this problem is actually very easy. All you got to do to begin with is turn off your furnace power switch." (Word of Advice TV, 3Jonl_TLkpE, [2:06], 140.71x)
   **Shape:** "very easy", then the first step is the safety step.
5. "Snow is not going to hurt it. Sun is not going to hurt it. Rain is not going to hurt it." (The DIY HVAC Guy, mP0IjyvQtxw, [2:09], 30.24x)
   **Shape:** three short "is not"s that answer the worry behind covering the unit.
6. "keep in mind your whole unit is designed to be outdoors get wet so none of this is really a hazard" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [4:51], 52.54x)
   **Shape:** water on the outdoor unit put in proportion, with the power already off.
7. "I hope you can see though that the space heater itself is not scary even these really cheap ones are designed and built to be extremely safe" (Technology Connections, HnMuNCl7tZ8, [21:40], 1.53x)
   **Shape:** the device cleared so the real risk (the outlet) gets the attention.

## 5. Promise blocks and concrete forward promises

Right after the point, two or three later payoffs, each naming its item and its stake (money, safety, the cold night). Notice that the good ones name a thing ("the last one", "the top three things"), that several put safety in the promise, and that none needs "stay". Borrow the placement (within about 30 seconds of the first answer), the count (two or three) and the item-plus-stake build.

1. "the last one will be the thing I think that affects your safety and your pocketbook the most" (HVAC Guide for Homeowners, Unx9Ze10N98, [0:08], 190.77x)
   **Shape:** one held item with two named stakes, safety and money. Mistake one follows at 0:17.
2. "I want to help you as a homeowner as a DIY learn how to check this item how to replace it yourself and how to do it safely" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Is0pv2Qnza0, [0:37], 60.42x)
   **Shape:** check, replace, safely: three promises, safety last.
3. "we're going to be showing the top three things that I find when I get called to go to a service call" (The DIY HVAC Guy, SkLMRM9NnBY, [0:45], 68.32x)
   **Shape:** the promise as the tech's own call log; paid as "those are the three things that I get called the most for".
4. "we're going to show you the good the better and the best option" (Home RenoVision DIY, J95l9Ue4224, [0:10], 24.92x)
   **Shape:** a three-rung ladder promised in one line; the prices for each rung come at about 16:30.
5. "so let's go through these tips and I'll show you what a difference they can make and at the end we'll do it after and see how we did" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [0:55], 52.54x)
   **Shape:** a before-and-after promised, paid with the vent reading at 8:31. Ours promises the viewer's own reading, not ours.
6. "I'm also going to rank each one of these brands from the premium line to the middle of the road line to the budget friendly line" (Atlas AC, r_uP9itJ0HQ, [2:20], 88.63x)
   **Shape:** the frame of the verdict promised, so the viewer knows how the list will sort.
7. "we're also going to talk about some different ways that you can save money in replacing your HVAC system that a ton of people simply don't know about" (The DIY HVAC Guy, x2BK-zr4raE, [0:13], 31.96x)
   **Shape:** a money promise beside the verdict promise. **Watch:** the source opens the block with "In this video, we're going to", a banned opener.

- **Problem:** "now I need you to stay tuned to the end because I got another tip for you" (Deanin' It Yourself, dRL13JlclhM, [0:43], 818.48x)
  A banned tease. The tip it hides (flush the removed piece too) is good and should be named in the promise.
- **Problem:** "closer to the end of the video I'm going to give you my top picks so you are going to want to watch this to the end" (Atlas AC, r_uP9itJ0HQ, [2:28], 88.63x)
  The verdict held to 12:01 behind a "watch this to the end".

## 6. Priority flags

One line at the first answer that tells the viewer which thing to act on if they act on only one. Notice that the real channels flag the part that decides the job ("almost guaranteed", "the number one most common failure") and give the floor for the viewer who won't do it all ("at the very least"). Borrow the placement (at the first answer, not minutes later) and the length (one short sentence, sometimes with the cost of getting it wrong).

1. "If you're seeing your furnace burners doing that when they only just come on for a couple seconds and go off, it's almost guaranteed that your problem is a dirty flame sensor." (Word of Advice TV, 3Jonl_TLkpE, [1:44], 140.71x)
   **Shape:** the symptom, then the cause flagged as nearly certain. Say it in the opening, not at 1:44.
2. "step number three is going to be cleaning the furnace and part of that is the number one most common failure that I see on a regular basis on a furnace and it is this flame sensor" (Everyday Home Repairs, --A2I2s7aNw, [3:09], 7.16x)
   **Shape:** the step flagged by how often it fails. (The guest is The DIY HVAC Guy.)
3. "but now let's talk about what is probably the number one repair or service call that is made and that has to do with this run capacitor" (How To Home, AQQH9QwC46A, [9:40], 11.05x)
   **Shape:** the flag by how often the call is made. (Capacitor work may be a tech's job for Roger; the profile decides.)
4. "So, do yourself a favor before it gets cold, go out and clean your flame sensor on your furnace and you should be good to go for the season." (The DIY HVAC Guy, mP0IjyvQtxw, [11:04], 30.24x)
   **Shape:** the one instruction with its deadline (before the cold).
5. "the first thing that you always want to make sure you do is disconnect power" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Is0pv2Qnza0, [0:46], 60.42x)
   **Shape:** the flag on the safety step, the first thing in the body.
6. "this single tip can make a giant difference in your air flow" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [2:37], 52.54x)
   **Shape:** the flag closing the filter tip, right after the swap.
7. "At the very least, change your filter twice a year." (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [3:16], 5.81x)
   **Shape:** the floor for a viewer who won't keep the full routine.

## 7. Item lines by shape

The body of the video, item by item. Five shapes recur. Notice that HVAC items run long (median 303 words on real channels), that the real channels give the setting, the wait and the order in plain words, that verdicts are said by who each option suits, and that a habit is respected before it's turned. Borrow the inner order and the length of each shape; rotate shapes across a channel's scripts.

**Method with settings and waits**

1. "You should go to your thermostat, turn the temperature down, wait 60 seconds, then turn off the power." (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [1:23], 5.81x)
   **Shape:** three actions and a wait, in order, in one sentence.
2. "all you got to do is turn that furnace power switch off for maybe five seconds and then turn it back on and that will reset it" (Word of Advice TV, 3Jonl_TLkpE, [2:36], 140.71x)
   **Shape:** the lockout reset: the switch, the wait, the result.
3. "let it run and sit there for like five to ten minutes until it's running crystal clear" (Deanin' It Yourself, dRL13JlclhM, [2:57], 818.48x)
   **Shape:** the wait as a range, with the sign that says stop.

**Rule, reason, verdict**

4. "The filter has arrows on it, and the arrow should always point toward the furnace." (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [2:01], 5.81x)
   **Shape:** the rule in one sentence, after the cost of breaking it.
5. "that requires 12 amps of current at 120 volts that is the maximum allowed to be drawn continuously from a typical 15a circuit" (Technology Connections, HnMuNCl7tZ8, [17:37], 1.53x)
   **Shape:** the number, then why it matters for the outlet.

**Contender verdicts**

6. "Now, this is tricky, but for most people with a 1-in filter, I just recommend a cheap fiberglass filter." (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [4:04], 5.81x)
   **Shape:** admits it's a judgement call, then the verdict for most people. Viewers lean the same way (cheap filters lead about 35 to 10).
7. "and to this day the difference in between carrier and Bryant is arguably nothing they come off of the exact same assembly line just with different labels and boxes" (Atlas AC, r_uP9itJ0HQ, [3:41], 88.63x)
   **Shape:** two contenders made one, with the reason.
8. "It could be more of a builder grade just by the materials that they use, but overall, it doesn't really matter. It still does the job" (The DIY HVAC Guy, x2BK-zr4raE, [4:23], 31.96x)
   **Shape:** the budget option's weakness named, then judged fairly.

**Myth, then truth**

9. "And that's a reasonable thing to think. It's a very expensive appliance, and we want to protect it. But, this is mistake number one, and here's why." (The DIY HVAC Guy, mP0IjyvQtxw, [0:57], 30.24x)
   **Shape:** the habit respected first, then turned. Covering the unit splits viewers about 52 to 25, so the respect matters.
10. "a lot of people are concerned about being too aggressive with the flame sensor and that's really not something that you have to worry about" (Everyday Home Repairs, --A2I2s7aNw, [4:24], 7.16x)
    **Shape:** the worry named, then cleared. (Word of Advice TV warns against sandpaper, group 11; where pros differ, the brief decides.)

**The escalation ladder**

11. "so you can try this and leave it at that but let's move on to doing a little bit more of an in-depth [fix] so that you won't have this issue again for a long time" (Silver Cymbal, qAxJb0J1HH0, [2:19], 46.03x)
    **Shape:** the quick fix is enough for some; the next rung is for the long term.
12. "Now, if you are really concerned about dust and air quality in the home, pick up a MERV 11, MERV 12, MERV 13 filter." (The Funny Carpenter, _g8gQ1gg1FM, [4:41], 5.81x)
    **Shape:** the stronger rung by need, with its cost said next ("more restrictive", "replace them more often").

## 8. The mechanism in one plain line

Why it works, in one sentence the viewer can repeat. Notice that the best ones use kitchen words (a battery, a bucket, an outside filter) and answer the "why" the symptom raises. Borrow the length and the placement (after the action, or as the answer to the viewer's question); one picture-phrase at most, and only when it teaches.

1. "And with time, when you have enough of a coating on here, it'll prevent the flame sensor from sensing any flame." (Word of Advice TV, 3Jonl_TLkpE, [3:44], 140.71x)
   **Shape:** the slow cause behind the symptom.
2. "the problem arises when this flame sensor gets dirty over the years and it thinks that there is no flame so it will turn the system off" (Everyday Home Repairs, --A2I2s7aNw, [3:50], 7.16x)
   **Shape:** the same cause told as the furnace's own mistake.
3. "your air handler is equipped with a safety switch on it to where if that drain pan fills up too high it will flip a switch that a lot of times then will cut power going to your thermostat" (How To Home, AQQH9QwC46A, [2:34], 11.05x)
   **Shape:** why a blank thermostat can mean a full drain pan.
4. "these pull air in all the time so they're almost like outside filters" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [3:09], 52.54x)
   **Shape:** the outdoor coil explained by the part the viewer already knows.
5. "And the thing is, air conditioners ARE heat pumps." (Technology Connections, 7J52mDjZzto, [1:40], 2.51x)
   **Shape:** the reveal in eight words; the rest of the video explains it.
6. "this is a high temperature limit switch it's an unassuming little fella but it's the reason why this plastic heater can be made cheaply yet also safely" (Technology Connections, HnMuNCl7tZ8, [5:44], 1.53x)
   **Shape:** the part, then what it makes possible.
7. "so you've got a heating and air system that at times is sort of dumping heat in a 5-gallon bucket then that 5 gallon bucket is dripping out the bottom if you will" (HVAC Guide for Homeowners, Unx9Ze10N98, [2:26], 190.77x)
   **Shape:** a leaky house as a leaking bucket.

## 9. Checks the viewer runs at home

A test the viewer can do in their own house, with what they'll see or hear either way. Notice that HVAC checks run on the senses (the fan, the hum, a drip, a blank screen, a warm plug), that the good ones name both results, and that none of the ones below needs a meter. Borrow the build (action, then "if this, then that") and the placement (at the step where the question comes up). Use only checks the brief confirms really work, and only on parts the persona may touch.

1. "if you can hear your gas valve opening, but the igniter was never glowing, then there's a pretty good chance that your igniter is the one that's actually bad." (Word of Advice TV, 1bRsFAMgZRQ, [4:02], 74.93x)
   **Shape:** a check by sight and sound, with no meter.
2. "you know that your drain is clogged because either you have water coming from underneath your AC unit or your thermostat is shut off and it's not coming back on" (Deanin' It Yourself, dRL13JlclhM, [0:21], 818.48x)
   **Shape:** two signs the viewer has already seen, either one enough.
3. "the rate the water's coming out right now is kind of slow so what that means is that I have a clog further up that pipe" (Silver Cymbal, qAxJb0J1HH0, [0:37], 46.03x)
   **Shape:** what the drip at the outside end tells you about the inside.
4. "a lot of customers they see a blank thermostat and they don't realize that there's batteries in the back" (Everyday Home Repairs, --A2I2s7aNw, [8:28], 7.16x)
   **Shape:** the free check before any call.
5. "in some instances the fan will be running but the compressor that buzz sound will not be happening" (The DIY HVAC Guy, Is0pv2Qnza0, [3:26], 60.42x)
   **Shape:** the symptom as two sounds at the outdoor unit. (Opening that panel may be a tech's job for Roger; the profile decides.)
6. "if you want to be extra safe feel how warm the plug is getting after the heater's been running for 10 minutes or so it's completely normal for it to be a little warm to the touch but if it's hot something's very wrong" (Technology Connections, HnMuNCl7tZ8, [22:22], 1.53x)
   **Shape:** action, wait, the normal result and the bad one.
7. "the number is not really super important what matters is is the difference" (Silver Cymbal, _b6p0fkWhCY, [0:30], 52.54x)
